name: Nora Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual day of work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Nora, 27, and I have a master’s in music. I lead the guitar chairs in a busy wedding band, record short music beds for local shops, and teach guitar on quiet afternoons. The best part is getting three generations onto the dance floor; the dull part is matching late invoices to old email threads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much room do you have if work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn well for a musician, saved roughly ten months of expenses, and there are plenty of bands and studios nearby. I live alone, though my parents are close enough for Sunday dinner. I use AI every day for schedules and rough demos, but I check every note before it reaches a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that routine paperwork finally got quicker, which is fine by me. The people at a wedding still expect a guitarist who can follow the room, not a perfect file on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income looks sound, and the savings let me turn down a badly priced date. I don't need AI to be a miracle; I need it to stop sending the same invoice twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the band dates, three teaching afternoons and shop recordings. This winter I'd learn a new AI invoice-matching feature on copies of my own records, check each result against the bank, and keep using it through the first year only if it catches errors without sharing customer details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about the work. Ten months of expenses saved and several nearby venues give me choices, though I still dislike chasing a fee after a Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your savings account buy you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cushion means I can refuse a shop that wants unlimited use for a one-day recording fee. I won't spend it on a new guitar just because a sales page says it is the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a new tool you would actually learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would learn the invoice feature rather than keep copying numbers by hand. I would stop if it mislabels a client's payment or sends their information outside my accounts.

say: I would welcome quicker **paperwork** while keeping wedding performances in human hands.
I would say a live guitarist must still **follow the room**.
think: Higher pay, nearby venues and **ten months saved** make routine changes manageable.
I want AI to fix **invoice errors**, not make grand promises.
do: Keep **band dates**, three teaching afternoons and shop recordings through the first year.
Learn a new **AI invoice feature** this winter on my own records.
Use it only after **bank checks** and only if customer details stay private.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and savings, despite chasing late fees.
S0.quote: The people at a wedding still expect a guitarist who can follow the room, not a perfect file on a screen.
fieldNote: Her **strong cash cushion** and high pay let her reject poor recording terms.
She already uses AI daily, but the **invoice feature** is a new, checked skill.

steps.text: Keep band dates, three teaching afternoons and shop recordings
Learn AI invoice-matching feature on own records and verify against bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say generated shop music will become cheap fast, and that is a fair challenge to anyone selling short recordings. My wedding band must earn its place by playing well and showing up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop beds could disappear first; they cover the gear and half my teaching-room rent. A good live season would help, but I would not pretend every Saturday is booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd learn a new AI audio-cleanup tool on my own takes and compare it with a paid engineer's result. In the first year, if shop orders fall, I'd offer a paid family-band workshop at the community centre only if the centre supplies a room and at least eight people book; I'd cut the room rental on empty weekdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about a real slice of pay, but I like a market that tells me when customers have moved. I have savings to test the next offer without borrowing against the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your business would feel the first cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop that now pays for a custom jingle may choose a cheap file, even if it sounds plain. I would count orders for two quarters before buying any new recording gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to buy equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mobile recorder costs more than one workshop earns. A new mobile recorder is not an investment until three paid workshop dates cover it.

say: I would accept cheap **shop music** as a real market challenge.
I would make the **wedding band** earn its fee through reliable live playing.
think: Shop recordings pay for **gear and room rent**, so fewer orders would hurt.
A strong **summer season** cannot guarantee enough winter dates.
do: Learn **AI audio cleanup** on own takes against a paid engineer’s result; buy recorder after three paid workshops cover it.
Offer **family-band workshops** if shop orders fall, a room is supplied and eight people book.
Cut **weekday room rent** in the first year if shop orders fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost recording pay, while willing to test another offer.
S1.quote: A new mobile recorder is not an investment until three paid workshop dates cover it.
fieldNote: Her **recording fees** support equipment and teaching space even though live work is strong.
She sets an **eight-booking threshold** and waits for three paid dates before buying a recorder.

steps.text: Learn AI audio cleanup on own takes; compare with paid engineer result
Offer paid workshop in first year if shop orders fall, centre supplies room and eight book
Cut empty weekday room rent in first year if shop orders fall
Buy mobile recorder only after three paid workshop dates cover its cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients that thinking AGI by 2028 could make our recording plans and shop tracks cheaply, while player-level robots follow around 2031. I would price the band for a human wedding, not pretend hands-on robots arrive in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recorded shop work and lesson plans might collapse in two years. My live guitar could still earn until 2031, but three wedding dates a month would not replace every weekday invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd separate wedding, lesson and recording money in my accounts and save a bigger share of shop fees. In the first year after AGI arrives, if shop orders halve, I'd stop renting the second recording room, run the family-band workshop only if eight people prepay and the centre offers a room, and audition for an open band chair if my own dates fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious, not lost. The savings buy time to ask what families still pay for, but the calendar would move faster than my usual way of testing a new show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would live weddings cover you between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weddings might carry me for three years, but summer dates do not pay every winter bill. The three years before robot guitarists arrive help my wedding band but do not protect my shop recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents if the studio side fell away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents that I have ten months saved and a plan to cut room rent before touching that account. I would ask them to listen to my new workshop, not to pay for it.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot players around 2031.
I would sell the band as a **human wedding**, not a file.
think: Cheap shop tracks and lesson plans could remove **weekday invoices** quickly.
Three wedding dates monthly may not replace **lost recording pay**.
do: Separate **income sources** and save a larger share of shop fees before 2028.
Stop renting the **second room** in first year after 2028 if shop orders halve.
Run **workshops** if shop orders halve with supplied room and eight prepayments; audition for open chairs if wedding dates fall.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with savings but little time to test a new show.
S2.quote: The three years before robot guitarists arrive help my wedding band but do not protect my shop recordings.
fieldNote: Her **2028 exposure** lies in recorded and planning work before robots play around 2031.
The **room cut**, prepaid workshop and audition each depend on actual lost bookings or paid demand.

steps.text: Save larger share of paid shop recordings before 2028
Stop renting second recording room in first year after 2028 if shop orders halve
Run workshops after 2028 if orders halve, centre supplies room and eight prepay
Audition for open band chair in first year after 2028 if wedding dates fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell other band leaders that five years is enough to build a better live service, and AGI in 2031 still comes before capable robots around 2034. A customer should know what is played by people and what comes from a file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a small roster of family workshops and wedding dates while recording still pays. I would not sink money into a studio if bookings do not prove the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd trial one paid workshop if the centre gives me a room and eight people prepay. Before 2031 I'd learn a new AI arrangement checker on my own wedding charts; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd keep workshops only if each covers the room, helper pay and my teaching time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recorded music prices, but I can test work one booking at a time. My father calls that keeping the roof before buying the sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count three fully paid workshop dates before buying the mobile recorder. Eight names on a workshop interest sheet would not be enough to spend savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many paid bookings would justify that investment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach younger guitarists to tune, listen and turn up for a job, then show them how to check an AI-made chart. The apprenticeship works only if there are paid dates where they can watch and help.

say: I would tell clients when **people play** and when music comes from a file.
I would use five years before **2031 AGI** to build a stronger live service.
think: Workshops and weddings could replace **recording pay** if customers book them.
A new **studio purchase** would be foolish without proven demand.
do: Trial a **paid workshop** this year with centre room and eight prepayments; buy recorder after three fully paid dates.
Learn a new **AI arrangement checker** on my own charts before 2031.
Keep **workshops** in first year after 2031 only when fees cover room, helper and teaching time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording prices, while testing one booking at a time.
S3.quote: Eight names on a workshop interest sheet would not be enough to spend savings.
fieldNote: She will **buy equipment** only after three fully paid workshop dates.
She sees **apprenticeship** as valuable only when a paid date covers the helper’s fee.

steps.text: Trial paid workshop this year only with centre room and eight prepayments
Learn new AI arrangement checker on own charts before 2031
Keep workshops in first year after 2031 only if fees cover room, helper and teaching time
Buy mobile recorder only after three fully paid workshop dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets a musician build real local customers and train young players without guessing every technical turn. Thinking AGI comes in 2036, while robots that can play follow about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be 37 when AI can plan and write at that level, and 40 when robot guitarists become possible. That is plenty of time to change my mix of work, but not a promise that every wedding will hire people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the band and lessons this year and save a share of every paid shop recording. Over the decade I'd take one apprentice on paid dates only after the booking covers their fee; in the first year after 2036 I'd keep live and teaching work that pays and seek an open music-centre post if wedding dates shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm with a long runway and a cash cushion. I still keep the workshop on a short lease because a popular class can turn quiet between terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a decade change how you teach younger players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show an apprentice how to read the room, not just how to press a button. I would pay an apprentice from a confirmed booking and never ask them to work for exposure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a cash cushion if you might invest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cushion lets me refuse a poor contract and pay an apprentice properly when the date supports it. It stays mostly in cash until customers, not forecasts, fund a change.

say: I would tell young players to build **local customers** and paid practice.
I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** separate from robot guitarists around 2039.
think: At **37**, I may lose planning work; at 40, robots could threaten live dates.
Ten years offers choices but no guarantee that **weddings hire people**.
do: Keep **band dates** and lessons this year while saving from paid shop recordings.
Take a **paid apprentice** on dates only when a booking covers their fee.
Keep live work after **2036** and seek an open centre post if dates shrink.
feel: I feel **calm** with time and savings, while keeping workshops on short leases.
S4.quote: I would pay an apprentice from a confirmed booking and never ask them to work for exposure.
fieldNote: Her **traditional outlook** favours paid apprenticeship and customer demand over promised support.
She keeps **cash reserves** until paid bookings justify change, despite a long preparation window.

Save share of each paid shop recording this year
Take apprentice on paid dates only if booking covers their fee
Seek open music-centre post in first year after 2036 if wedding dates shrink

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording orders could halve before my workshop has a paying crowd. A centre room at a price eight customers can cover and clear information on open band chairs would help. I can use my savings, but I want the next service to pay its own way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether young players get paid while learning. I can talk about a community of musicians all day. An apprentice still needs bus fare and supper.

headlineQuote: An apprentice still needs bus fare and supper.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old guitarist** with a master’s degree who leads wedding players, records shop music and teaches.
Her **higher pay**, ten-month cushion and plentiful nearby jobs support careful experiments without borrowing.
She uses **AI daily**, yet learns new features on her own material and checks privacy and results.
Fast AGI threatens **shop recordings** before robot players arrive; she tests prepaid workshops and paid apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could halve shop recording orders before workshops have paying customers.
whatWouldHelp: A **centre room** priced for eight prepaid customers would support a workshop trial.
Information on open **band chairs** would help if wedding dates also fall.
